file.content:
\paragraph{Ablation confirms routing function.}
We ablate attention to instruction tokens at the readout position.
Ablating all 24 dominant heads at L1 increases action $R^2$ by $+0.042$ (baseline $0.517$)\footnote{$R^2$ values differ from Table~\ref{tab:rsa_overview} due to the feature reconstruction pipeline; all comparisons are within-experiment.}.
We compare against 10 random subsets of 24 heads (Appendix~\ref{sec:random_subset_ablation}): random ablation yields a larger mean increase of $+0.077 \pm 0.013$ ($z = -2.73$, $p = 0.003$).
Dominant heads produce a smaller gain because they carry organized routing signals (structured noise for the probe); random heads lack such organization.
In the original extraction pipeline (\S\ref{sec:repr_extraction}), L1 ablation increases $R^2$ by $+0.059$ vs.\ no-ablation baseline, decaying at deeper layers (L8: $+0.018$; L13: $\Delta \approx 0$); instruction routing is an entry-layer phenomenon.

\paragraph{Action trajectory validation.}
Ablating 24 instruction-dominant heads alters $72.3\%$ of action tokens ($d = 0.65$); control ablation (8 heads) yields $d = 0.41$ ($29.3\%$), concentrated on the gripper dimension (shift $0.291$ vs.\ $< 0.034$; Appendix~\ref{sec:action_trajectory}).

\paragraph{Dose-response gradient.}
Ablating 4--32 instruction-dominant heads yields monotonic divergence ($d = 0.482 \to 0.639$; Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}), with steep rise through 12 heads and plateau beyond 20 (Appendix~\ref{sec:action_trajectory}).

\paragraph{Counterfactual instruction analysis.}
To test instruction dependence, we replace the original instruction with four perturbation types.

The ordering follows semantic distance from the original instruction.
L1 ablation ($d = 0.65$) falls between shuffled and paraphrased, consistent with removal of instruction signal rather than injection of noise (Appendix~\ref{sec:action_trajectory}).
